# Draft:Mel King (The Pitt)

Mel King is a fictional character from the HBO Max medical procedural drama The Pitt, portrayed by actress Taylor Dearden. Mel was introduced in "7:00 A.M.", where she begins her first day working in the emergency department of Pittsburgh Trauma Medical Center. Throughout the day, Mel proves herself to be a compassionate, competent doctor who cares deeply for her twin sister Becca. In the show's second season, her relationship with Becca is further developed while Mel simultaneously struggles to cope with being named in her first medical malpractice lawsuit.
Mel is implied to be autistic. The characterisation of Mel and her portrayal by Dearden, a neurodivergent actress, has received praise from critics and audiences.
Character biography
Season 1
Mel is introduced as a bright, enthusiastic second-year resident who has previously worked in a VA hospital. Alongside Victoria Javadi, Dennis Whitaker and Trinity Santos, it is her first day at the emergency department of Pittsburgh Trauma Medical Center.
Mel tends to the case of Ginger Kitajima, an elderly woman who has schizophrenia. She recognises the signs of caregiver stress shown by her daughter, Rita, who Mel advises to take a break from her responsibilities. Mel worries that her advice may have backfired when Rita disappears, seemingly abandoning Ginger. When Rita returns, Mel and social worker Kiara Alfaro offer caregiver support resources.
Mel bonds with Dr. Frank Langdon and works with him frequently throughout the day. When Langdon struggles to treat Terrance Swedeen, an autistic man who injured his ankle while playing table tennis, Mel assists by dimming the room's bright lights and shutting the door to quieten the loud noises of the emergency department. She openly communicates with Terrance and pays attention to his concerns. This approach calms Terrance and impresses Langdon. Mel reveals to Langdon that she has an autistic sister named Becca and that her experiences of caring for her informed her communication approach with Terrance.
When a six-year-old drowning victim dies after an unsuccessful attempts at resuscitation, Mel comforts the victim's younger sister Bella. The case upsets Mel. Langdon comforts her, and assigns her the job of extracting gravel from a patient's road rash, which she is pleased to do.
Mel competently responds to the onslaught of PittFest shooting victims that arrive at the emergency department. Supervising Whitaker and Santos, she treats the victims with extremity wounds. Faced with dwindling blood supplies, she successfully convinces Dr. Robby to allow her and other members of staff to donate blood to the victims. During the chaos, Mel manages to reunite a mother and daughter who had been separated during the shooting. Robby praises her work.
Working with Dr. John Shen, Mel performs a lumbar puncture on a patient with measles, pneumonia and sepsis. The procedure had been approved by the patient's father but the mother disapproves and orders for it to stop. Mel discretely manages to complete it.
At the end of the day, Mel leaves the hospital and collects Becca from her care facility. The season ends with Mel initiating their weekly ritual of eating dinner at a restaurant and then watching a movie.
Season 2
The second season resumes ten months later on the 4th of July. Mel spends the day worrying about a malpractice lawsuit related to the lumbar puncture she performed in the first season; her deposition is scheduled to take place in the afternoon. She zones out while with patients and struggles to answer questions during a trauma procedure. Noticing her nerves, Robby and Dr. Baran Al-Hashimi offer encouragement, and, after her own deposition, Dr. Parker Ellis pulls Mel side with advice about what to expect.
Some flirting from a patient distracts Mel from her deposition. However, he turns out to be a criminal, and, while running from the police, he pushes Mel, who falls and hits her head against the floor. While examining her injury, Langdon confesses to his drug addiction and apologises for letting her down.
Almost immediately prior to being summoned for the deposition, Mel's stress accelerates when Becca arrives as a patient. Mel asks Langdon to oversee her care. After finishing her deposition, Mel asks Langdon for the details of Becca's health, though Langdon refuses to disclose anything, citing HIPAA. Becca tells Mel that she has a urinary tract infection and that she has a boyfriend who she has been having sex with. Mel responds poorly, distressed that Becca had hidden this from her.
Mel additionally helps Dr. Samira Mohan provide care for an elderly couple that supports their limited mobility while respecting their autonomy, and reassures Langdon when he questions if he is ready to return to work.
Development
Mel's character was developed with advice from Dr. Wendy Ross, a developmental and behavioural paediatrician who also serves as the director of the Jefferson Center for Autism and Neurodiversity. It was Ross' suggestion to not explicitly confirm an autism diagnosis for Mel within the show in order to reflect the high rates of autistic women who are diagnosed later in life or not at all. Ross also recommended that a neurodivergent actress should be cast in the role.
Dearden has stated that her performance was informed by her own experiences of having ADHD. While filming the first season, she approached Noah Wyle with the suggestion that Mel should work well during emergencies, something that she has described as "a very real ADHD thing". Dearden had previously been disappointed by the portrayal of neurodivergent characters as emotionless and the usage of neurodivergence for comedic effect in most general media.
Dearden has also said that she plays Mel as an asexual character. Amid speculation about Mel's relationship with Langdon (played by Patrick Ball), Dearden felt that it was more powerful for their relationship to remain platonic, stating in an interview with Screen Rant, "we [Dearden and Ball] thought we were portraying a unique thing to see on TV, because you always see shipping, but you don't see platonic friends."
Reception
The portrayal of Mel's neurodivergence has been widely praised. Placing Mel in contrast with the character of Dr. Shaun Murphy from The Good Doctor, Sarah Kurchak wrote for Time, "I often sense that autistic and autistish characters are more of a collection of random traits shoehorned into a vaguely human-shaped cog in a story than a fully realized component of a series or film. Mel, on the other hand, strikes me as a complete person whose traits are part of a greater whole." Her general compassion and the intuitive care she showed towards Terrance Swedeen in season one has also has received approval.
The decision to cast a neurodivergent actress to play Mel has also been praised.
